title: Tempo, mood and takes; Norvo's avoided clichés
summary: Takes differ with tempo and emotion; he once planned twenty trademark licks to be recognized but never played one.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Another thing you said, Red, was you said -- you know, you said each take would be different, you know you said she just sang from the heart and it came out -- it never -- it wasn't a set performance, at anytime.

No, no. It was always different that way and I think that's -- that was a great thing about her too, the tempo or anything -- we'd take a thing and attempt a tune with an arrangements and we'd be taking maybe the wrong thing, there was a wrong feel for the tune -- so we'd kind of listen and -- maybe this thing would go a little better slow. Maybe it would, we'd say, why don't we try it. So we'd take five -- and we'd come back and we'd decide on a tempo maybe the first take would be right.
Yeah.
And we'd just go down, that'd be it.
Yeah.
Just conception of what --
Yeah.
-- where the thing was and we weren't really well enough known with the tune to pick that tempo. But she had a feel for everybody, I think.

But you had another thing to say about that, Red, you said -- when you were talking about playing from the heart and playing from inspiration and everything, you said finally -- you were talking about yourself, too, and you said funnily enough, I mean, you're not always going to play that same number at that same tempo. Cause you're not always going to feel the same way.

Well I think that's the beautiful part of improvising and jazz, it's -- music is that it's never going to quite be the same. She never -- really going to play it -- you might lead into a chorus, I've heard guys lead into a chorus the same way, maybe on a certain thing, because it feels right it seems to give the sled a push for them.
Yeah.
Then go on. I've heard little thing like that happen. But a change of tempo from night to night, or the way you feel, will alter what you play.
Yeah.
Now you know, years ago, when I first

started to record, I used to think, you know, when I hear oh, a certain clarinet player or this trombone player I recognize him immediately. Now why? What is there about him that I recognize? He does something that's always the same, that I recognize that it's him instead of somebody else.
Yeah.
You know possibly the two clarinet players I know or three clarinet players that play, or the three or four trombone players that are different that you --
Yeah.

-- recognize. So I thought, should I -- so this is kind of a like a -- oh, kind of a dare to myself, I though, yeah. So I got about 20 clichés, so to speak, and the -- endings, the way I'd finish, you know.
Yeah, identification.
Yeah, I think, well if I use these, and use these different times, they're going to say hey that's --
Hey that's got to be Red.
That's him on xylophone, that's him.
Yeah.
You know I never could play one of those. Not one. I get in the studio, start out playing and everything and I'd finish the date and said, 'What happened?' I never played one of them. (laughter)
Well you know that that could've hindered
you terribly anyway. Cause if you -- that could've hindered you --
Oh, it's like having a --
Being in a straitjacket or something.
Sure, it's like a straitjacket, there's no way you could move.
NO.
You can't sit back and wait that, you gotta flow into these things.
Sure, that's right.
I remember, after two or three times, oh, that'll never happen -- going to play a bad chorus.
